3. The High Court Division while issuing the Rules in the writ petitions called upon the appellants (review petitioners)hereof, who were respondents in the writ petitions, to show cause as to why the respective orders passed by them on different dates directing to make assessment of Customs duties and taxes on the imported goods of the respective writ petitioners as per the tariff value fixed therefore, in view of the issuance of the notification being SRO No. 113-AIN/97/1705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997, by which the applicability of the scheme of CRF has been withdrawn from the imported goods in question, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 4. The case of the respective writ-petitioner-respondents were that they opened their respective letters of credit when the Preshipment Inspection of Goods Rules 1996, issued under Section-25A of the Customs Act, 1969 vide SRO No. 244-Ain/96/1693/Shulka dated 31.12.1996 (here-in-after referred to as SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 or the Rules, 1996) containing schedule-1 therein, was in force and the schedule-1 of the said Rules, 1996 contained a list of 12 importable items, which were kept out of the benefits of the CRF scheme. The respondents opened their respective letters of credit for import of items, not included in the schedule- I of the aforementioned SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996, and as such the imported goods were entitled to the benefits of the CRF scheme. Accordingly after inspection of such imported goods at the loading port, the CRF Certificates were duly issued by the government approved Preshipment Inspecting Agency complying with the provisions of the Rules, 1996 prior to the date of issuance of the S.R.O. No. 113-Ain/97/1705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997, published in the Gazette on 13.05.1997 (hereinafter referred to as SRO No. 113 dated 13.05.1997), by which the imported goods in reference along with some other imported goods were included in the list of schedule- I of S.R.O. No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 and thereby the imported goods were barred from getting the benefits of the CRF scheme with effect from 13.05.1997, as the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 was published in the Gazette on 13.05.1997, and that the imported goods in reference were, however, saved and entitled to get the benefits of the CRF scheme, since the CRF certificates were issued in terms of the SRO Nos. 113 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 32.12.1996. The respondents hereof having opened the letters of credit long before the issuance of SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, which came into effect from 13.05.1997 as aforementioned, the writ petitioners acquired vested right to be assessed on the basis of the value certified in the CRF certificate issued under Section 25A of the Customs Act, and that the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 could not take away such vested right of the importer-respondents in view of the principles as laid down in the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, 48 DLR (AD) 199 and also the judgment dated 11.05.1998 passed by this Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 6, 7, 8, 10, 11 and 12 of 1995. 

 5. Before the High Court Division on behalf of the writ respondents it has been submitted that in view of the provisions of Sections 30 and 30A read with Section 25(7) of the Customs Act, 1969, the Government has power to fix the tariff value of the imported goods, and the imported goods were to be assessed on the basis of the tariff value prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry and that on behalf of the writ petitioners it has been submitted that with the introduction of Tariff value under Sections-25(7) and 30A of the Act the restriction put on by Section 30 of the Customs Act, 1969, for determining the normal value of the imported goods as prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry has been relaxed and that the non obstante clause, as appearing in section 25A of the Customs Act, 1969, made its application overriding all other sections of the Customs Act, 1969 and that the writ petitioners opened the letters of credit relying on the declaration of the government made vide SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 issued pursuant to Section-25A of the Act, 1969, assuring release of the imported-goods, on payment of the Customs duty and other charges to be assessed on the basis of the value of the imported-goods verified and certified in the CRF Certificates issued by the government approved Pre-shipment Inspection Agents against payment of their required fees and charges, and that the importer-writ petitioners: got their goods inspected by the government approved Pre-shipment Inspection Agents (PSI Agents), on payment of their required fees and charges, as per SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and the Rules, 1996 framed and issued under Section-25A of the Act and that thereby the writ petitioners have acquired vested right to have the customs duty assessed on their imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificated value duly issued by the government approved PSI Agents. 

 6. The High Court Division on due consideration of the submissions made on behalf of the contesting parties and relying on the principle laid down in the decisions given by Appellate Division in the cases of Collector of Customs Vs. A. Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167; Collector of Customs Vs. Ahmed Hossain reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199; and Mostafizur Rahman Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40 made the Rules issued on the writ petitions absolute holding that the respondents thereof acted illegally, arbitrarily and without lawful authority in refusing to assess the Customs duty, tax etc. on the imported goods on the basis of the value mentioned in the CRF Certificates issued by the PSI Agents and that the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 could not affect the vested right accrued to the respondents on the issuance of the CRF certificates pursuant  to SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 issued under Section 25A of the Customs Act. 

 7. This Division in disposing of the said civil-appeals preferred against the aforesaid judgments passed in writ petitions by the High Court Division making the Rules absolute considered the submissions of the appellants that the imported goods in reference, subsequently being included in the list of schedule-1 of SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996, vide SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, were taken out from the benefit of CRF Scheme, and those not being case of withdrawal, reduction or exemption of the duty under section 19 of the Customs Act, the decisions reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 were not applicable in the appeals and that the High Court Division committed error of law in making the rules absolute relying on the aforesaid decisions, and that the imported goods having been excluded from the purview of the CRF scheme, introduced under section 25A of the Customs Act, vide SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, the value of the imported goods after said date i.e. 11.05.1997 were to be assessed in terms of section 25(1) and (2) read with Section-25(7) of the Customs Act as contemplated by the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act and as such the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the duty on the imported goods were to be assessed on the basis of CRF certificated value of the goods issued in accordance with law and that the appeals were fully covered by the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149. 

 9. During admission hearing of the review applications it has been submitted by the learned Advocates appearing for the review-petitioners that on the issue involved in the review applications, conflicting decisions have been given by this Division and the decision of this Division being the law of the land it is necessary that this Court need reconsider the issue raised and lay down the correct exposition of the law to be followed by the Courts and Tribunals of the Republic and that this Division finding substance thereon was pleased to grant leave to review the issues involved in the appeals in the following terms:- 

 "We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners and the contents of the petitioners. It has been submitted that the Appellate Division missed the question of law that the issue of effective date of value and vested right to such value was determined by the Appellate Division in the case of Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 wherein their Lordships held that the importer had no vested right so far value of import is concerned and that the said judgment was delivered by five Hon'ble Judges and that the Appellate Division comprising 3 Judges in effect overruled the said decision of 5(five) Hon'ble Judges and thus such overruling of the decision of a larger Bench is an error of law apparent on the face of the record. 

 11. In the (review) appeals the issue to be answered is whether the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) certificates issued, under Section-25 A of the Customs Act read with SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and S.R.O. No. 244 dated 31.12.1996, as were in force till the date of withdrawal of the benefit of CRF scheme from the imported goods in reference through inclusion of the said imported goods in the list of schedule-1 of SRO No. 244-Ain/96/1693/Shulka dated 31.12.1996 along with some other items, vide SRO No. 113-Ain/971705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997 published in the gazette on 13.05.1997, thereby making the said SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 effective on and from 13.05.1997, and presented before the customs authority for the purpose of assessment of duty under Section-30 of the Act after 13.05.1997, are binding on the appellants hereof, since the importers relying on the declaration given by the government vide S.R.O. Nos. 316 dated 3.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 pursuant to Section-25A of the Act, 1969, opened their respective letters of credit incorporating therein the condition of obtaining CRF certificate as mentioned in the said SROs and procured the CRF certificates in accordance with law and thus acquired vested right, to get their respective imported goods to be assessed on the basis of the CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997 and whether the CRF certificate issued validly under Section-25A of the Act supersedes the tariff value fixed under Section 25(7) of the Act. 

 12. The learned advocates for the review-appellants submitted that in deciding the cases of (1) Abdul Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167, (2) Ahmed Hossain reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199, (3) Mostafizur Rahman reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40 and (4) Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 this Division has settled the law that the importers cannot claim any vested right on the value of the imported goods or the rate of duty thereon on the basis of the value of goods or rate of duty, as the case may be, prevailing on the date of opening of the letters of credit and that the provisions of Section-30 of the Customs Act, 1969 have to be followed for determination of the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of Custom's duty, tax etc. It has been submitted that the value of the imported goods and the rate of duty as prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry along with all required documents and papers before the Customs authority for assessment of the duty, tax etc., shall be the value of the imported goods and the rate of duty to he imposed on such goods as per Section-30 of the Customs Act and there is no confusion on this issue. 

 13. The learned Advocates referring to the judgment under review dated 13.07.2002 submitted that in fact the same has overruled the decision reported in 52 DLR (AD) 49 (judgment dated 01.06.2000) and that their lordships must have inadvertently overlooked the fact that the said decision, reported in 52 DLR,  has been passed by a Bench consisting of 5 Judges whereas the judgment under review is given by a Bench consisting of three Judges and that in the facts, and circumstances it was necessary to get the appeals under review heard and disposed of by a Bench consisting of at-least five Judges. The learned Advocates then submitted that in the instant case admittedly on the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry under reference, the imported items were taken out of the CRF Scheme vide SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 and therefore on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry the CRF certificates issued in respect of the imported goods had no legal binding .inasmuch as with the withdrawal of the benefit of the CRF scheme from the imported goods, those goods fell under the purview of Section-30 of the Act and the mere issuance of the CRF Certificate cannot put a bar as per the principle of estoppel, since there cannot be any estoppel against statue. Section 30 of the Customs Act provides the date for determination of the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of Customs thirty and since the imported goods under reference were taken out of the purview of CRF scheme as far bad (on 13.05.1997, the importers are not entitled to ally benefit on the basis of the CRF certificates issued in respect of the consignments of which the Bills of Entry were submitted on 13.05.1997 or thereafter. The learned Advocates submitted that due importance should be given to the date mentioned in Section 30 of the Customs Act, the parent statute for determination of the "value of the imported goods and the rate of duty" to be imposed thereon. The value of the imported goods is to be determined as per Section-25(1) & (2) of the Customs Act, in the absence of existence of tariff value fixed as per Section 25(7) of the Customs Act, and that in terms of Section 30 of the Customs Act existing tariff value was to be treated as the value of the imported goods, on the basis of which customs duty was to be assessed, but their lordships in the judgment under review failed to consider this aspect of the law and the fact that with the withdrawal of CRF benefit from the consignments under reference, the binding force of CRF certificate ceased and the tariff value in force has to be taken into consideration for the purpose of assessment of the customs duty and thus their lordships arrived at an erroneous decision. The learned advocates referred to the judgment and order dated 26.04.2007 passed in the case of Commissioner of Customs Vs. Unita International (Civil Appeal No. 55 of 2001) heard and disposed of along-with about 374 appeals, on the same issue, by a Bench of this Division consisting of five Judges, wherein it has been held that the assessment of Custom duty, has to be made on the goods-imported in terms of normal value or tariff value, as the case may be, as per provisions of Section 30 read with Sections-25 (1) & (2) and 25(7) of the Customs Act and that though the L.Cs were opened prior to 13.05.1997 the importers cannot claim any vested right for assessment of customs duty on their imported goods, on the basis of CRF certificates issued after issuance of the SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997, and that the rejection of the CRF value by the Customs Authority has been made in view of existence of the tariff value, which is within the valid jurisdiction of the Customs Authority, and submitted that in view of the principles laid down in the said judgment dated 26.04.2007, and being the latest judgment on the issue, the judgment of the appeals under review cannot be sustained and is liable to be set aside. 

 14. On the other hand Mr. Abdur Razzaq, the learned Advocate appearing for the importer-respondents, submitted that the importers having opened their respective letters of credit incorporating the condition of obtaining CRF certificate relying on the declaration given by the government vide SRO No. 316-Ain/94/1568/Shulka dated 03.11.1994, and in terms of SRO No. 244-Ain/96/1693/Shulka dated 31.12.1996, as were in force, and accordingly the importers having got their imported goods duly inspected and the required CRF certificates issued therefore, by the government approved PSI Agents, against payment of the prescribed fees and charges, in compliance to the said SROs, such importers acquired a vested right to get the assessment of the Customs duty and charges on the imported goods on the basis of the value mentioned in the CRF certificates, at least which were issued prior to issuance of SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997. 

 15. The learned Advocate also submitted that the date fixed for determination of the value of the imported goods mentioned in Section 30 of the Customs Act has been relaxed for two specific situations, one is when Tariff Value, fixed under Section 25(7) of the Customs Act, is in force and the other is when the verified and certified value of the imported goods is mentioned in the CRF certificates issued under the authority of Section 25A of the Customs Act complying with the provisions of the SRO Nos.  316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996. Section 25(7) of the Customs Act has provided for fixing an unified rate of value of any imported goods, to avoid the discrepancies in the determination of the customs duty having regard to the value of the goods imported from different countries with different rates of price prevailing at the relevant time, that is to say, that on any specific imported goods there may be different procurement prices in different countries on the same day and on importation of such goods procured at different prices will cause different valuation of the imported goods creating differences in the assessment of customs duty. The government in order to avoid the same, on collecting prices of the same goods imported from different countries, fixes a common price as value of such imported goods in terms of Section-25(7) of the Customs Act, for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty and such fixed common price is known as Tariff Value and that such Tariff Value, till modified or altered, is applied to all such imported goods without question as to the procurement price of the individual importers and such fixation of tariff value has facilitated and simplified the assessment process of Customs duty and clearance of the imported goods. Such Tariff Value superseded the provision of Section-30 of the Act, as was in force, at the relevant time. 

 16. Thus the tariff value as fixed is not the contemplated value of the imported goods prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry as per Section-30 of the Customs Act. The tariff value though fixed at an earlier date but has been accepted as the value of the imported goods on the date of presentation of the relevant Bill(s) of Entry, provided such goods do not come within the purview of CRF scheme. The value of imported goods mentioned in CRF certificates has been made acceptable for the purpose of assessment of the Customs duty, provided such imported goods were not listed in schedule 1 of SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996. 

 17. The learned Advocate then submitted that the CRF certificate scheme has been introduced by the government to have a check on the importation of proper goods by the  Government approved agents, who/which were authorized to inspect and certify the description, quality, quantity and value of the goods-imported at the loading port complying with the provisions of SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 and. the government has assured, declaring through said public notifications, that such CRF certificates shall be accepted for the purpose of determination of the value of the imported goods in assessing the customs duty. Such the CRF Certificated value supersedes the value mentioned in section 30 of the Customs Act inasmuch as Section 25A has been given an overriding force over all the Sections of the Customs Act, thereby the provisions of Section 25A overrides the provisions of Section 25(7) as well as Sections 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. It has been submitted that the assessment made by the PSI agents is also based on Section 25(1) and (2)of the Customs Act giving due importance to the price prevailing in the countries from which procured in certifying the value of the goods after being loaded in the vessel for import purpose. 

 "to consider the submissions that the High Court Division erred in law making the Rules absolute ignoring that Section 25A of the Customs Act relates to the value on the basis of which the goods imported are to be assessed and it has nothing to do with exemption in the rate of duty and the CRF facilities under Section 25A having been withdrawn before the presentation of the Bills of Entry Provisions in Section 30 of the Customs Act were applicable and accordingly the customs authority rightly refused to assess the duty on the basis of Certificates and the High Court Division, without taking into consideration the provision of Section 25(1), 25(7), 30 and 30A of the Customs Act, erroneously held that the respondents acquired vested right on the opening of the letters of credit." 

 and their lordships in the said judgment (Unita case) have held that: "In the present cases, the respondents claim legal/vested right on the ground that at the time of opening the letters of credit they could get the imported goods assessed on the basis of CRF and subsequently by different notification the above privilege was withdrawn/cancelled but as it appears in 52 DLR (AD) 49, the Appellate Division held no vested right accrued even though at the time of opening of the letter of credit there was a notification (SRO) providing for lesser tariff value. So there is no question of acquiring vested right by the respondents merely on the basis of such SRO's relying on which they opening their letters of credit:" 

 19. and thus it appears that the decision in the "Unita International" case is based on the date of opening of the letter of credit, which is not the case in the appeals under review. Further the judgment under review has not been considered in deciding the said "Unita International" case. 

 20. We have perused the impinged judgment and considered the submissions of the learned advocates of respective parties. It appears that though Section 30 of the Customs Act provides that the value of the imported goods to be the value prevailing as normal price as per Section 25 (1) & (2) of the Customs Act, on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry, for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty, yet the government has made relaxation in aforementioned two circumstances namely in case of existence of the tariff value fixed under Section 25(7) of the Customs Act and in case of furnishing CRF certificate issued pursuant to Section 25A of the Customs Act complying with SRO Nos. 316 dated 3.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996. 

 21. In the instant cases after opening their respective LCs the importers complying with the terms of the LCs and provisions of the SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 issued under Section 25A of the Customs Act, got the imported goods inspected by the duly approved Government PSI agents on payment of the prescribed fees and charges, and obtained the required CRF certificates, thereby as per the assurance given by the government vide S.R.O. Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 pursuant to Section-25A of the Custom Act, which is an independent promise of the government, the CRF Certificates issued in terms thereof became binding on the Customs authority, thereby such importers have acquired a right to get their imported goods assessed for payment of Customs duty On the basis of the value certified in the CRF Certificates. 

 "It has been recognized by superior Courts of the sub-continent that specific assurance made by the government may give rise to equitable protection under promissory estoppel. The question is whether a notification under section 25A of the Customs Act gives rise to a vested right and protection under promissory estoppel. Section 25A amended till 1995 provides that the price verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved reshipment inspection agency will he accepted as the basis for assessment and the price under this section means the value of the goods determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of Section 25. The respondents relying on the notification under this section acted to their detriment by having their goods inspected by inspectors appointed by the Government and by incurring expenses for such inspection. Would in such special circumstance of Government's assurance that the price so determined by the inspection would be accepted by them as the basis for assessment create a vested right? Would it be inequitable and unjust to allow the government to treat such inspection certificate as an idle exercise and a scrap of paper having no value at all? The promise of accepting the price having been made by the appellant under a law, should the Government by bound by such a promise when the other side has acted bonafide and to his detriment relying on that promise?" 

 "Doctrine of promissory estoppel has been variously called 'promissory estoppel' requisite estoppel, quasi estoppel and new estoppel'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppel', is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppel. The true principle of promissory estoppel seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or affect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealings which have taken placed between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppel need not be inhibited by the same limitation as estoppel in the strict sense of the term. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason, logic or principle why promissory estoppel should also not be available as a cause of action, if necessary to satisfy the equity." 

 24. We are in respectful agreement with the analysis as made by their lordships of this Division, in the body of the impugned judgment of the appeals under review, quoted above, and rely on the same for consideration of the issue on the certificated value. 

 25. It appears that at the relevant time the value of any imported goods could be determined in three different ways on the date of presentation of the Bills of Entry i.e. (i) one being the value to be determined following the provisions of Section-30; (ii) the second one being the tariff value, fixed pursuant to Section 25(7) of the Customs Act; and (iii) the third one is the value certified in the CRF Certificate issued by a government approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency following the provisions of SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 issued pursuant to section 25A of the Customs Act. Having regard to the non-obstante clause appearing in Section 25A of the Customs Act the CRF certificated value of the imported goods overrides all other modes for valuation of imported goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duty on such imported goods. The value of the imported goods certified in the CRF Certificate relates to the date of issuance of the CRF certificate, and not to the date of opening of L/C or the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry as per Section-30 of the Act. 

 26. It appears that in deciding the appeals under review their lordships have considered the application of CRF certificates having regard to the date of opening of letters of credit but not the date of issuance of the CRF certificates, (emphasis given) as contemplated by the provisions of Section 25A of the Customs Act and the declaration given by the government therefore vide SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996. The CRF Certificates have been issued against payment of fees/charges by the respective importers to the government approved PSI agents, who inspected the imported goods at the port of loading and issued the CRF certificates in accordance with law. 

 27. The provisions of Section-25(7) of the Act for fixation of tariff value goes to show that the Government may fix a value of imported item(s) and until such value is altered or changed, though fixed at an earlier point of time, is accepted by Customs Authority as the value of the goods, in place of the value calculated as per Section 25(1)and (2) read with Section-79 of the Customs Act, as prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry in terms of Section-30 of the Act, inspite of the fact that there may be differences in between the Tariff value in force, fixed as per Section-25(7) of the Act, and the value calculated as per Section 25(1) and (2) of the Act, prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry, as per Section-30 of the Act. Similarly in view of the CRF scheme, the value certified in the CRF certificate on the date of issuance of the certificate is accepted as the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty in view of the declaration given by the government vide SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994. It is to be noted that the Bill(s) of Entry is/are naturally presented sometime after the date of issuance of the CRF certificate, since it takes time to reach the goods at the port of discharge, and the CRF certificate is issued on inspection of the imported goods at the port of loading before the vessel sails there from, and that the value of the imported goods may vary on the date of submission of the Bill of Entry in usual course. Since the importer has acted on the assurance and declaration given by the government under the CRF scheme vide SRO No. 316 dated 3.11.199.4 the value of the imported goods as mentioned in CRF Certificates has been accepted for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty by the customs authority on presentation of the Bill of Entry with such CRF certificate issued at an earlier date. The importers having acted upon the assurance of the government such CRF certificated value becomes effective for the purpose of assessment of the customs duty, no matter when the Bill of Entry with such CRF Certificate is presented. As per SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 the CRF certificate becomes effective once it is issued, provided on the date of issuance of the certificate the imported item comes under the purview of the CRF scheme and the law permits issuance of such CRF Certificate on such date. The Customs authority has accepted this position and acted accordingly and made assessments of Customs duty on the imported goods on the basis of CRF Certificate issued earlier to the date of submission of the Bill of Entry. Thus it appears that for the goods-imported covered by CRF scheme, the date of issuance of the CRF Certificates actually matters for the purpose of assessment of Customs duty and not the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry. Therefore even if the imported item is taken out from the purview of CRF scheme with effect from 13.05.1997, any CRF certificates issued prior to said date in accordance with law is valid and is binding on the Customs authority, no matter when the relevant Bill of Entry is presented for the purpose of assessment of duty. In the instant cases where the CRF certificates were issued prior to 13.05.1997 in respect of the imported items, not included in the list of schedule-1 of the SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 prior to 13.05.1997, those are not debarred from getting benefit of the CRF scheme. The SRO No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 cannot affect the CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997 inasmuch as with the issuance of CRF certificate the transaction is complete and closed and is binding on all concern, since the parties concern have performed their respective obligations in the issuance of the CRF certificates. 

 (2) Section-25(7)-"Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the Government may by notification in the official Gazette, fix, for the purpose of levying customsduties, tariff values for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty advalorem; Provided that any imported or exported goods the declared value of which is higher then its tariff value fixed under this subject section shall be chargeable with customs duty on the basis of its declared value." 

 (3) Section-30-"Date for determination of the value and rate of import duty-(1) The value of and the rate of duty applicable to any imported goods shall be the value and the rate of duty in force-in the case of goods cleared for home consumption under section 79, on the date on which a bill of entry is presented under that section; in the case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption under section 104, on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse; and in the case of any other goods, on the date of payment of duty;" 

 (4) Section-30A- "Value and effective rate of duty- Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any Court, for the purposes of Section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively  include the value as determined under Section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under Sections 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duty that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale of such goods of opening of a letter of credit in respect of thereof." (5) এস, আর, ও নং ৩১৬-আইন/৯৪/১৫৬৮/শুল্ক-dated 03.11.1994-Customs Act, 1969 (IV of 1969) এর section 25A তে প্রদত্ত ক্ষমতাবলে সরকার ঘোষণা করিল যেঃ- 

 29. On a careful examination of the aforesaid provisions, quoted hereinabove, it appears that Section 25A has non-obstante clause by which the provisions of Section 25A overrides all other Sections of the Customs Act, thereby the provisions of Section 25A will prevail over all other provisions of the Customs Act, 1969 including those of Section 25(7) as well as Sections 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. It further appears that Section 25A provides that the Government may by notification in the official gazette, declare, amongst others, the price of any imported goods verified in the prescribed manner (i.e. mentioned in a CRF Certificate by an approved. Pre-shipment Inspection Agency) shall be accepted as the basis for assessment of Customs duty and pursuant to that provision of Section-25'A of the Customs Act, the government issued the SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994, quoted above, wherein the Government has categorically declared that the price of any imported goods verified and certified by an approved Reshipment Inspecting Agency shall be the basis for assessment of customs duty, subject to compliance of the provisions of the SROs i.e.-Clauses-1(Kha), 2(2),2(4) and 13 of SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and Clauses; 79(Kha), (Uma), (Dha) of SRO No. 244, dated 31.12.1996. Such declaration of the government is independent of all other sections of the Customs Act. Thus it is clear from the aforesaid provisions of Section 25A read with those of SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 that the value of any imported goods verified and certified by an approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency shall be the basis for assessment of the customs duty inspite of the existing provisions of Sections 25(7) (for fixing Tariff value) and Section-30 of the Customs Act and that there is no restriction as to the date of presentation of the Bill of Entry accompanying the CRF certificates issued for the purpose of assessment of custom duty or as to expiry of the validity or effectiveness’s of such CRF Certificate(s) once issued. 

 30. Section 25(7) provides for fixation of tariff value by the Government following the procedure laid down therefore and that such tariff value, as may be fixed, unless altered or modified, prevailing on the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry, shall be the value of the imported goods, subject to the overriding provisions of Section 25A of the Customs Act read with SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 i.e. CRF certificates issued thereunder, for the purpose of assessment of customs duty. 

 31. The value of the imported goods certified and verified in the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) Certificate issued by 'the government approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency under Section-25A of the Act shall be the value of the imported goods for the purpose of assessment of the customs duty and shall be binding on the customs authority superseding the Tariff value fixed under Section-25(7) of the Act and or the normal value, if any fixed under Section-15(1) &(2) read with Section-79 as per Section-30 of the Act. It further appears from the provisions of SRO No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and SRO No. 244 dated 31.12.1996 that such Clean Report of Findings Certificate is issued by the government approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agencies only on payment of the required fees and after inspecting the goods at the port of loading certifying, amongst others, the value thereof and such CRF Certificate being issued as per the declaration made by the Government to the effect that "Section-25A তে প্রদত্ত ক্ষমতাবলে সরকার ঘোষনা করিল যে -----” and “------প্রদত্ত প্রত্যয়নপত্র শুল্কায়নের ভিত্তি হিসাবে গৃহীত হইবে।”  vide SRO No. 316 dated 03.11:1994 pursuant to Section 25A of the Customs Act, such certified value becomes binding upon the customs authority to admit and accept the said value as the value of the thwarted goods, when the Bill(s) or Entry is/are presented, for assessment of Custom's duty. Thus once a CRF Certificate is issued by an approved Pre-shipment Inspecting Agency, complying with said SRO Nos. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and 244 dated 31.12.1996 such certificate becomes binding on the authority for the purpose of assessment of the duty, etc. inasmuch as such CRF certificated issued under section-25A overrides the provisions of Section 25(7) and Section 30 of the Customs Act in view of the nature of the non-obstante clause appearing in Section-25A of the Customs Act. 

 32. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we do not find any substance on the submission of the learned Advocates appearing for the review petitioner that with the inclusion of the imported items in reference in the list of schedule-1 of S.R.0.244 dated 31.12.1996, vide S.R.0.113 dated 11.05.1997, such item(s) is/are not entitle to the benefit of CRF Certificate scheme if the relevant Bill(s) of Entry is/are presented after 13.05.1997 for assessment of customs duty. It is also submitted that in view of the principle that there is no estoppel against statute and the provisions. of Section-30 of the Customs Act has retrospective effect, the CRF certificates under reference have lost their effectiveness with the inclusion of the imported goods in schedule-1 of S.R.O.244 dated 31.12.1996 vide SRO 17, No. 113 dated 11.05.1997 with effect from 13.05.1997 and hence the orders as passed by the Customs authority refusing to accept the CRF certificates are in accordance with law. But in the facts and circumstances, said principle of estoppel is not applicable in the instant case, particularly in view of the overriding provision of Section-25A read with the declaration given, by the government vide S.R.O. No. 316 dated 03.11.1994 and the importers having acted on such declaration of the government, the CRF certificates became effective on the date of issuance thereof and remains valid. There is no mention of any date in the law as to the expiry or validity of such CRF certificates. 

 33. The judgment of "Unita International" (being C.A. No. 55 of 2001) disposed of along with other 747 Civil Appeals; dated 26.04.2007 appears to be inconsistent with the provisions of Section-25A of the Customs Act as was in force. The words "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act" appearing in section 25A goes to show that the application of said Section-25A supersedes all other sections of the Customs Act and shall accordingly prevail over the tariff value fixed under Section 25(7) of the Act and also the provisions of Sections 30 and 30A of the Act. 

 "Since the concept and definition of normal price and tariff value have distinct meaning with separate legal interpretation as to its aspects and application for the purpose of determination of value for assessment of duty of any goods under import, the customs authority on receipt of a Bill of Entry, first of all, is bound in law to ensure whether the goods having respective H.S. Code falls under prevailing tariff value notification and if it is so, as was found in many of the writ petitions, are to treat those goods as per section 25(7) because of the fact that tariff value supersedes the concept as well as application of normal price under Section 25(1) & (2) and 25A. So if any goods which fall under tariff SRO of a relevant period shall straightway attract the provision of Section 25(7). Therefore, only on items of import which does not fall under tariff value notification of a relevant period can be treated under Section 25A if it does not attract tariff value and this treatment of valuation implies pure and simple determination of normal price under Section 25(1) and (2) read with 25A as the case may be. Accordingly the determination of normal price and tariff value, as in the above writ petition, nullifies the pleas of the respondents for acceptance of CRF under section 25A. The cancellation of CRF value is done in pursuance to tariff SRO which is within the valid jurisdiction of the appellant. The claim of the writ petitioner respondents to the date of opening letter of credit has got no relevance arid, material footing in these cases of the writ petitioner respondents because if any consignment in question is subject to treatment under section 25(7) there lies no room for attracting the provision of section 25(1) & (2) read with section 25A whatsoever." 

 35. Goes to show that the tariff value fixed under section 25(7) of the Customs Act supersedes the CRF .value certified under Section 25A of the Customs Act but the law as discussed hereinabove is otherwise. 

 36. On careful perusal of Section 25(7) and 25A of the Customs Act reveals that Section 25(7) override of all other sub-sections of Section 25 of the Customs Act only, whereas Section 25A overrides all other Sections of the Customs Act and thereby the CRF value certified validly under Section 25A overrides any tariff Value fixed under Section 25(7). Therefore it cannot be said that only the items of import which do not fall under tariff value notification of a relevant period can be treated under Section 25A and that if any imported goods fall under tariff SRO of a relevant period shall straightway attract the provision of Section 25(7) Provisions of Section-25A of the Customs Act supersedes, the Provisions of Section-25, which includes Section-25(1) & (2), 25(7), 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. CRF; certificates issued validly shall get preference and the value certified therein shall supersede the value of the imported goods fixed under Sections 25(1) & (2) and or 25(7) of the Customs Act and shall be binding on the Customs authority. Thus the goods imported with CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997 shall get the benefit of the CRF scheme and such goods shall be assessed for customs duty on the basis of the CRF certificated value. 

 37. Thus the Customs duty of the imported goods, the value of which have been duly verified and certified by the government approved by Pre-shipment Inspecting Agencies at the port of loading prior to 13.05.1997; the publication date of the SRO No. 113-Ain/97/1705/Shulka dated 11.05.1997 in the official gazette, should be assessed on the basis of such CRF certificated value and that Section 30 of the Customs Act will not affect the value of such imported goods certified in the CRF certificates issued prior to 13.05.1997, inspite of withdrawal of such goods from the benefit of CRF scheme effective from 13.05.1997 i.e. prior to the date of presentation of the Bill(s) of Entry to the Customs authority, for assessment of Customs duty.
